_comment: Varicose veins. Same architecture as pneumonia: shared surgery and core skills carry the examination, the disease adds reflux mapping as its mechanism, CEAP as its severity anchor, and fitness-for-intervention as its management decision. Subtitle names the two eponymous tests.
name: Varicose veins
subtitle: Trendelenburg and Perthes tests
oneLine: Leaking leg valves mapped by hand and duplex, from compression and habits to ablation

chapters.title: Basics
chapters.blurb: What a varicose vein is, which system it runs in, and whether anything drives it

chapters.title: Patient particulars
chapters.blurb: Age, sex and work set the odds before the leg is exposed

skill.particulars.demographics.expect: In suspected varicose veins, middle age, female sex with pregnancies behind her, and a job done standing all day carry real weight. Note the occupation precisely: conductors, police and traffic staff, nurses, hawkers and farm workers bring the classic story, and a loaded bowel habit or a pelvic lump in the same history changes the whole workup.

chapters.title: History of presenting illness
chapters.blurb: Evenings, not mornings, and relief on lying down

skill.hx.chief_complaints.expect: A typical presentation reads in years with an evening rhythm: heaviness and aching for years, worst at day end after standing, gone by morning. Bursting pain on walking, sudden hot cord pain, or bleeding episodes break that rhythm and each points away from simple primary disease.

skill.hx.surg.varicose_veins.expect: Expect aching heaviness with evening ankle swelling, night cramps and itching over the lower leg. Press for the three complications the skill lists: burst bleeding, red tender cords, and skin sores, and for the deep thrombosis history that decides whether surface surgery is even allowed.

chapters.title: Past, personal, drug and family history
chapters.blurb: The risk factors that decide primary against secondary

chapters.title: General examination
chapters.blurb: A well patient, and the abdomen that must not be skipped

skill.gen.appearance.expect: Expect a generally well patient with a chronic complaint, not an acutely unwell one. Build, gait and footwear still matter: obesity loads the veins, and a tiptoe gait held for years can shorten the Achilles tendon above a chronic ulcer.

skill.gen.vitals.expect: Vitals are usually normal and that normality is a finding: it places the case on a routine list. Fever with a hot red leg means superimposed thrombophlebitis or cellulitis, not simple varices, and hypotension with bleeding means the ruptured varix is the emergency.

skill.gen.edema.expect: Expect pitting ankle oedema that gathers through the day and largely clears overnight. Non-pitting swelling with thick toes points to lymphoedema instead, and whole-limb swelling with a tense calf points to deep venous disease.

chapters.title: Examination of the veins
chapters.blurb: Standing inspection, two named tests, and the pulses that clear compression

skill.exam.surg.varicose_inspection_palp.expect: Expect tortuous great saphenous trunks on the inner leg and thigh, or small saphenous trunks up the back of the calf, with a saphena varix coughing expansively at the groin and fascial pits over medial perforators. Grade the gaiter skin as you go: pigmentation, eczema, woody thickening, white patches, healed scar or open ulcer.

skill.exam.surg.trendelenburg_tourniquet.expect: Expect a double answer in the classic case: slow filling from below while the junction is held proves the perforator leak, and a rush from above on release proves the saphenofemoral leak. One without the other still localises treatment, so observe the two phases separately and report them separately.

skill.exam.surg.perthes_deep_vein_patenc.expect: Expect the varicosities to empty as the patient walks with the surface trunk occluded, with no calf pain. That emptying is the single result that clears the leg for ablation or stripping, and bursting pain with further distension forbids it outright.

skill.exam.surg.arterial_pulses_lower.expect: Pulses must be documented because compression and ulcer care depend on arterial supply. Palpable dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses with no claudication story clear the way for stockings; absent pulses or claudication demand an arterial index before anything is wrapped.

skill.exam.surg.regional_nodes.expect: Inguinal nodes are usually impalpable in simple varices. Enlarged tender nodes mean an infected ulcer, and enlarged hard nodes with a long-standing odd-edged ulcer raise the question of malignant change and need tissue diagnosis.

stations.title: Examine the varicose leg
stations.task: This 44 year old woman constable has had left leg varicose veins for six years with evening heaviness. Examine her lower limbs and present your findings with the system involved.
examinerQuestions: Your thumb control is held and the veins still fill from below. Where is the leak, and what operation must include it?
On walking with the tourniquet on, her calf bursts with pain and the veins distend further. What has this proved, and what is now forbidden?
You see a saphena varix at the groin. How do you separate it from a femoral hernia without any instrument?

stations.title: Take a venous history and triage
stations.task: This 52 year old bus conductor has prominent leg veins and ankle swelling toward evenings. Take a focused history in six minutes and be ready to say whether this looks primary and what test comes first.
examinerQuestions: Which four facts in his story would make you suspect secondary disease, and what would you examine next?
He reports a white painful swollen leg after a long journey five years ago. How does that change your plan?
Name the single investigation that maps treatment and the bedside index needed before compression.

skill.reasoning.varicose.basics.title: What varicose veins are
skill.reasoning.varicose.basics.oneLine: Dilated surface veins from leaking valves, in one of two saphenous systems, primary or secondary
skill.reasoning.varicose.basics.why: The word varicose describes a shape, but the disease is a pressure: blood falling back down the leg through valves that no longer close. Until you can say which valves leak, in which system, and whether anything higher up is driving the pressure, you cannot choose between a stocking, a needle and an operation.

teach.heading: A varicose vein is a failed valve, not just a big vein
teach.body:
A vein is called varicose when it is dilated and tortuous. In the leg this happens because valves in the surface system, or at the junctions where surface meets deep, stop closing and let blood fall back down the leg. The pooled column raises surface pressure, and the raised pressure stretches the vein wall further, so leak and dilatation feed each other.

That is why the symptoms follow posture: standing fills the column and the leg aches, while lying down drains it and the ache lifts. Any pain that ignores posture is unlikely to be venous at all.

rows: Great saphenous
From in front of the medial malleolus, up the inner leg and thigh, to the groin
Saphenofemoral junction near the groin
Small saphenous
From behind the outer ankle bone, up the back of the calf, to behind the knee
Saphenopopliteal junction in the popliteal fossa
Perforators
Short links through the deep fascia, mainly on the inner calf and thigh
Join surface trunks to the deep veins

teach.heading: Primary disease and secondary disease behave differently
teach.body:
In primary disease no outside cause is found: the surface valves or the vein wall itself are at fault, often with a family pattern, and often brought out by standing work, weight or pregnancy. Most clinic cases are of this kind.

Secondary disease has a driver: deep valves wrecked by an old thrombosis, outflow blocked by pregnancy or a pelvic or abdominal lump, or rarely a congenital shortcut pouring arterial flow into the veins. Find the driver before touching the surface veins, because removing them can remove the only way home the blood has.

teach.heading: Who gets it
points: Middle-aged adults most often, and women more often than men, with pregnancy a common trigger.
Workers who stand all day: conductors, police and traffic staff, nurses, hawkers and farm labourers.
Anyone with a mother or sisters affected, which points to inherited wall or valve weakness.
The obese, in whom raised abdominal pressure loads the leg veins.
Anyone with a past deep vein thrombosis, whose damaged deep valves breed secondary varicosities.

pitfalls: Treating the visible vein as the disease and the tests as decoration, when the junction and the deep veins decide the treatment.
Calling every tortuous leg vein primary without asking after thrombosis, pregnancy, pills and the abdomen.
Promising that removing surface veins cures heaviness that never varied with posture.

probes.q: What makes a leg vein varicose, in one mechanism?
probes.a: Incompetent valves let blood reflux down the leg, and the resulting venous hypertension dilates the superficial vein until it is tortuous.

probes.q: How does the course of small saphenous varicosity differ from great saphenous varicosity?
probes.a: Great saphenous varicosity runs up the inner leg and thigh to the groin, while small saphenous varicosity runs up the back of the calf from behind the outer ankle to behind the knee.

probes.q: Why must secondary varicosities be excluded before surface surgery is offered?
probes.a: When deep veins are blocked or a higher obstruction drives the pressure, the surface varicosities carry essential return flow, and removing them risks severe congestion and ulceration.

sources.source: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.reasoning.varicose.signs.title: The varicose picture
skill.reasoning.varicose.signs.oneLine: Evening heaviness, a standing examination, two named tests, and skin that keeps score
skill.reasoning.varicose.signs.why: Every finding in chronic venous disease is one story told twice: high surface pressure first stretches the vein, then injures the skin it feeds. A student who reads symptoms, tests and skin as chapters of that single story will localise the leak and grade the disease at the bedside; one who memorises them separately will mix up the tests and miss the ulcer that is coming.

teach.heading: The evening leg
teach.body:
The classic story is an aching heaviness of the whole leg or the lower leg, worst toward the end of the day, worse after long standing, and relieved by lying down. Night cramps, ankle swelling that gathers through the day, and itching over the lower leg complete it.

Two pains warn of something else: a bursting pain on walking points to deep venous blockage, and sudden severe pain with a hot red cord points to superficial thrombophlebitis. Neither belongs to simple primary disease.

teach.heading: Read the leg standing
teach.body:
Veins collapse flat, so the leg must be examined standing with groin-to-toe exposure. Trace which trunk is diseased, look for a groin bulge that coughs expansively, feel for pits in the deep fascia where perforators leak, and study the gaiter skin above the ankle for pigmentation, eczema, thickening or ulcer.

A saphena varix that fills on coughing means the saphenofemoral valve has failed. Fascial pits mark the perforators that are pumping deep pressure outward, and each one is a site the treatment must close.

teach.heading: Bedside tests and what each answers

rows: Cough impulse at the groin
Expansile thrust felt over the saphenous opening
Saphenofemoral valve incompetence
Trendelenburg, pressure released
Veins fill in a rush from above
Saphenofemoral reflux confirmed
Trendelenburg, pressure held
Veins fill slowly from below despite control
Incompetent perforators below the control
Perthes walking test
Veins empty and the calf stays comfortable
Deep veins open, surface work is safe
Perthes walking test
Veins distend further with bursting calf pain
Deep blockage, surface surgery forbidden

teach.heading: Skin changes are the clock
teach.body:
Long pressure leaks red cells and fluid into the gaiter skin: first brown pigmentation, then eczema, then a woody thickening of skin and fat with white starved patches, and finally a shallow ulcer above the inner ankle that follows trivial injury or nothing at all.

Bleeding from a surface varix can be alarming but is controlled by lying flat with the leg raised and firm direct pressure, never by a tourniquet round the limb. A non-healing or odd-edged ulcer with enlarged groin nodes needs biopsy, since long-standing venous ulcers can rarely turn malignant.

pitfalls: Examining the leg on the couch and declaring the veins mild, when standing would have shown the full disease.
Confusing a saphena varix with a femoral hernia: the varix vanishes on lying down and coughs expansively.
Applying compression or booking ablation without checking pulses and the arterial index first.

probes.q: What single feature of the ache most strongly suggests venous disease?
probes.a: It worsens with dependent standing through the day and is relieved by lying down with the leg raised.

probes.q: With thumb control held at the groin, the veins still fill from below on standing. What does this prove?
probes.a: Incompetent perforating veins below the control are filling the surface system from the deep veins despite saphenofemoral occlusion.

probes.q: Why does a normal Perthes test clear the leg for surface surgery, from first principles?
probes.a: Emptying of the varicosities during calf exercise with the surface trunk occluded proves the deep veins are open and the calf pump clears them, so the deep system can take over all return flow.

sources.source: Browse's Introduction to the Symptoms and Signs of Surgical Disease
sources.locator: Varicose veins: symptoms and bedside tests

skill.reasoning.varicose.differential.title: What else swells, stains or ulcerates the leg
skill.reasoning.varicose.differential.oneLine: Deep disease, lymphoedema, arterial disease and malformations beside simple varices
skill.reasoning.varicose.differential.why: Most tortuous leg veins are exactly what they look like, but the ones that are not carry the danger: a blocked deep system that forbids surgery, an ischaemic leg that forbids compression, and a lymphoedematous leg that needs a wholly different service. The differential exists to protect the treatment, not to decorate the diagnosis.

teach.heading: First separate primary from secondary
teach.body:
Before naming mimics, decide whether the varicosities are primary or driven. Sudden onset, one-sided whole-limb swelling, a past white painful leg, a pelvic lump, or bursting pain on walking all argue that deep thrombosis or outflow obstruction is driving the picture, and duplex of the deep system comes before any surface plan.

Primary disease, by contrast, builds over years, favours both legs or at least the standing worker symmetrically, eases overnight, and shows a clean abdomen with open deep veins on testing.

rows: Deep venous insufficiency after thrombosis
Whole-leg swelling, bursting pain, woody skin, past white leg
Perthes worsens, duplex shows deep damage
Lymphoedema, including filarial disease
Non-pitting swelling, thick toes, no venous reflux pattern
Stemmer sign, normal duplex, dorsum of foot involved
Superficial thrombophlebitis
Hot red tender cord along a known varix
Localised along vein track, vein feels firm and tender
Arterial disease with ulceration
Claudication, pale pulseless foot, ulcer on toes or shin
Low ankle-brachial index, compression forbidden
Cellulitis of the leg
Acute hot spreading redness with fever
Hours to days, not years; veins may be normal
Congenital malformation with fistula
Young patient, limb overgrowth, thrill and bruit
Continuous murmur on auscultation over the veins

teach.heading: Traps in our clinics
points: Filarial lymphoedema is common in endemic districts: a big non-pitting leg is not venous until duplex says the veins leak.
A pelvic fibroid, ovarian cyst or cervical growth in a middle-aged woman can present as new one-sided varicosities: examine the abdomen in every new case.
Eczema over varicosities gets potent steroid creams from many hands: ask what has already been applied before judging the skin.
An ulcer above the middle third of the leg, or one that is deep, punched or foul in a new way, is not a venous ulcer until other causes are excluded.

pitfalls: Labelling a post-thrombotic leg as primary varices and booking ablation into a blocked deep system.
Putting compression on an ischaemic leg because the ulcer was assumed venous without an arterial index.
Missing a pelvic cause in a woman because the examination stopped at the groin.

probes.q: Name three conditions that mimic varicose veins with swelling or ulceration.
probes.a: Deep venous insufficiency after thrombosis, lymphoedema, and arterial disease, with superficial thrombophlebitis and cellulitis as acute mimics.

probes.q: How do you separate lymphoedema from venous oedema at the bedside?
probes.a: Lymphoedema is non-pitting with thickened toes and a positive Stemmer sign and involves the dorsum of the foot, while venous oedema pits, gathers through the day, and spares the toes with reflux demonstrable on duplex.

probes.q: A 58 year old woman has new one-sided varicosities with whole-leg swelling. What must you exclude and how?
probes.a: Secondary obstruction from a pelvic or abdominal cause such as a fibroid, ovarian cyst or nodal mass, by abdominal and pelvic examination with duplex of the deep system before any surface treatment.

sources.source: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery
sources.locator: Varicose veins: differential diagnosis of leg swelling

skill.investigation.varicose.workup.title: Mapping the reflux before treating it
skill.investigation.varicose.workup.oneLine: Duplex maps the leak, the arterial index clears compression, and the grade is recorded
skill.investigation.varicose.workup.why: The hand localises the leak but cannot see it: it cannot tell a junction leak from a perforator leak with certainty, and it cannot see the deep veins at all. Duplex draws the map the intervention follows, and the arterial index is the gate before compression, so ordering them is not thoroughness but safety.

teach.heading: Duplex maps, the hand only suggests
teach.body:
Duplex ultrasound traces reflux down the great and small saphenous trunks, marks the failed junctions, finds the incompetent perforators, and checks that the deep veins are open and their valves work. The old tourniquet tests taught generations where to look, but the map for ablation or surgery is drawn by duplex, not by thumb pressure.

Order it standing or with provocation, and ask the reporter for exactly what the intervention needs: which junctions reflux, how far down each trunk the reflux runs, which perforators leak, and whether the deep system is patent.

teach.heading: The arterial index before any compression
teach.body:
Measure the ankle-brachial index before a compression stocking or bandage goes on any leg, and always before treating an ulcer. A significantly low index means arterial disease shares the leg, and compression then risks starving the skin it was meant to heal.

Where duplex or Doppler measurement is unavailable, palpable pulses with no claudication history offer a rough bedside screen, but they do not replace the index where compression or intervention is planned. Refer for measurement rather than guessing.

teach.heading: Document and look upstream
points: Record the CEAP clinical class and photograph the leg, so progress and recurrence are judged against a baseline.
Examine the abdomen and pelvis whenever onset is sudden, one-sided, or late in life, and arrange pelvic imaging where a lump is felt.
Take a formal deep thrombosis history with every duplex request: an old white leg changes what the scan must answer.
Send routine fitness blood tests only when intervention is planned, not as a substitute for the map.
Red flags that jump the queue: burst bleeding, a hot tender cord tracking toward the groin, a rapidly spreading ulcer, or a cold pale foot.

pitfalls: Booking ablation on clinical tests alone, then finding deep disease or a missed perforator when the veins return.
Compressing an ulcerated leg without an arterial index, and converting venous disease into ischaemic loss.
Ordering venography or cross-sectional imaging routinely when duplex already answers every needed question.

probes.q: What four facts must the duplex report give before intervention?
probes.a: Which junctions reflux, how far down each trunk reflux runs, which perforators are incompetent, and whether the deep veins are patent with working valves.

probes.q: Why is the ankle-brachial index mandatory before compression?
probes.a: A low index reveals coexisting arterial disease, and compressing an ischaemic leg risks skin necrosis and ulceration instead of healing.

probes.q: Duplex is unavailable at your centre and the leg needs compression for an ulcer. What do you do?
probes.a: Check pulses and claudication history as an initial bedside screen, withhold compression until arterial disease is formally excluded, dress the ulcer, and refer early to a centre with Doppler measurement and duplex mapping.

sources.source: Browse's Introduction to the Symptoms and Signs of Surgical Disease
sources.locator: Varicose veins: duplex assessment and the arterial index

skill.reasoning.varicose.diagnosis.title: Naming the disease and grading it
skill.reasoning.varicose.diagnosis.oneLine: Primary or secondary, the system, the CEAP class, and fitness for intervention
skill.reasoning.varicose.diagnosis.why: Saying varicose veins names a shape, not a plan. The surgeon needs to know whether the disease is primary or driven, which trunk and junction leak, how far the skin has travelled toward ulceration, and whether the deep veins will carry the leg after surface work, and all of that belongs in one diagnostic sentence.

teach.heading: Name four things in one sentence
teach.body:
A complete diagnosis states primary or secondary disease, the trunk and junction involved, the CEAP clinical class, and the current state: uncomplicated, with skin changes, with healed ulcer, or with active ulcer. Each part changes management, so a diagnosis missing any part is unfinished.

Fitness for intervention is part of the statement, not an afterthought: deep veins shown open by history, Perthes and duplex, and arterial supply checked, so the leg is declared fit for ablation or surgery in the same breath.

teach.heading: What the CEAP classes mean tonight

rows: C2
Varicose trunks without swelling or skin change
Stockings and habits, ablation if symptomatic
C3
Venous swelling of the ankle and leg
Compression becomes central, map the reflux
C4
Pigmentation, eczema or woody thickening
Treat skin, close the leak, watch closely
C5
Healed ulcer held closed by care
Lifelong maintenance compression
C6
Open ulcer in the gaiter zone
Multilayer compression with wound care, urgent reflux plan

teach.heading: A worked statement
teach.body:
Primary varicose veins of the left great saphenous system with saphenofemoral and Cockett perforator incompetence, CEAP C4a with pigmentation and eczema, deep veins patent, arterial supply adequate, fit for duplex-mapped ablation.

Contrast the secondary form: secondary varicosities of the right leg following documented deep vein thrombosis, deep system damaged, surface veins acting as collaterals, not for ablation, for compression and vascular follow up. The two sentences look alike and prescribe opposites.

pitfalls: Stopping at varicose veins without saying primary or secondary, leaving the most dangerous question unanswered.
Quoting a CEAP class without the skin findings that earned it, so nobody can verify the grade.
Declaring fitness for ablation on clinical tests alone, before duplex has confirmed open deep veins.

probes.q: What four parts belong in a complete varicose vein diagnosis?
probes.a: Whether disease is primary or secondary, which trunk and junction are involved, the CEAP clinical class, and the current state with fitness for intervention.

probes.q: What separates CEAP C4 disease from C6 disease, and why does it matter?
probes.a: C4 is skin change without an open ulcer while C6 is an active gaiter ulcer, and C6 needs multilayer compression with wound care plus an urgent reflux plan rather than routine ablation booking.

probes.q: Duplex shows a damaged deep system with surface collaterals. State the diagnosis and the consequence.
probes.a: Secondary varicosities with deep venous damage acting as collaterals, which forbids surface ablation and commits the leg to compression with vascular follow up.

rubric.text: States primary or secondary with the evidence for it
Gives the CEAP class with the findings that earn it
Declares fitness for intervention with deep and arterial checks

skill.treatment.varicose.management.title: Managing varicose veins
skill.treatment.varicose.management.oneLine: Compression and habits first, ablation for truncal reflux, surgery where ablation cannot reach
skill.treatment.varicose.management.why: Varicose veins return whenever the leak is left open and the habits unchanged, so treatment is a ladder, not a single procedure: habits and compression settle symptoms and protect skin, closing the reflux stops the pressure, and surveillance keeps the gain. Starting on the wrong rung means an ulcer that heals and returns, or veins stripped that should have been ablated.

teach.heading: Conservative care first, and always alongside
teach.body:
Offer graduated compression stockings, regular leg elevation, walking and calf exercise, and weight reduction first, especially where intervention is declined or unsafe. Compression eases heaviness and swelling, protects eczematous skin, and is the base on which ulcers heal.

Check the arterial index before any compression goes on. Teach bleeding safety early: lie flat, raise the leg, press firmly on the bleeding point, and seek care, with no tourniquet round the limb at any stage.

teach.heading: Close the reflux: ablation first
teach.body:
Map every leak with duplex first. For reflux in the great or small saphenous trunk, endovenous thermal ablation by laser or radiofrequency is the first-line closure, with ultrasound-guided foam sclerotherapy and open flush ligation with stripping as alternatives where ablation is unavailable or unsuitable.

Treat incompetent perforators feeding skin change or ulceration as part of the same plan, since leaving them open is how ulcers return. Secondary disease with a damaged deep system is not for surface closure at all.

teach.heading: Skin, ulcer and bleeding
teach.body:
Treat venous eczema with emollients and topical corticosteroids alongside compression, and treat gaiter ulceration with multilayer compression and wound care rather than bed rest alone. Most venous ulcers heal under good compression once the arterial supply is confirmed.

Refer urgently for burst bleeding that will not settle, a hot tender cord tracking toward the groin, rapidly spreading skin change, or an ulcer that looks atypical or refuses to heal, since long-standing ulcers need assessment for deeper causes.

teach.heading: Referral and follow up in our setting
points: Refer to vascular services for symptomatic trunks, progressive skin change, healed or active ulcer, bleeding varices, or superficial thrombophlebitis near the junction.
Where ablation is unavailable or unaffordable, well-done stripping with perforator attention at a government surgical unit remains sound care: say so plainly.
Keep compression going after any procedure and review for recurrence, which is commonest where deep disease coexists or stockings are abandoned.
Counsel standing workers on sitting breaks, elevation, weight and exercise: the job that made the veins will unmake the repair.
Safety-net every patient on bleeding control and ulcer warning signs before they leave the clinic.

pitfalls: Ablating or stripping without duplex mapping, and leaving the feeding perforator or a second trunk behind.
Compressing without an arterial index, or advising stockings a patient cannot afford without naming the cheaper alternative.
Discharging a healed ulcer without maintenance compression and surveillance, and meeting the same ulcer next year.

probes.q: What is the first-line closure for great saphenous trunk reflux?
probes.a: Endovenous thermal ablation by laser or radiofrequency after duplex mapping, with foam sclerotherapy or open ligation with stripping as alternatives.

probes.q: A varix bursts at home and bleeds heavily. What should the family do?
probes.a: Lie the patient flat, raise the leg above heart level, press firmly on the bleeding point, and seek urgent care, with no tourniquet round the limb.

probes.q: Why does a venous ulcer need compression even after the reflux is closed?
probes.a: Residual venous hypertension and coexisting deep disease keep driving recurrence, so maintenance compression with surveillance holds the healing that the procedure started.

sources.source: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery
sources.locator: Varicose veins: conservative and operative treatment

skill.treatment.varicose.management.dosingNote: This module teaches management at the level of modality and principle: compression, elevation and habits first, ablation for truncal reflux, sclerotherapy or surgery as alternatives, and compression-based ulcer care. Specific agents, strengths and durations come from your current national or institutional guideline at the time of treatment. CliniX does not prescribe.

cases.title: A constable with six years of evening heaviness in the left leg
cases.opening: Sunita Pawar, 44, has come to the surgical outpatient clinic after her traffic duty shift. She stands through most answers and keeps shifting her weight off her left leg. Introduce yourself and take a history.
cases.fallback: I am not sure what you mean, doctor. Can you ask that a different way?

patient.name: Sunita Pawar
patient.occupation: Traffic police constable, on point duty through the day
patient.residence: Urban, lives with her husband and two children in Pune

cues: what brings you here today
tell me about the trouble in your leg
what is the main problem today
presenting.reply: Doctor, the veins of my left leg have become thick and twisted over six years, and the leg feels heavy every evening after duty.

cues: when did the veins first appear
how has the swelling progressed over the years
has the condition worsened with time
onset_course.reply: Small blue lines showed behind my calf about six years back. They grew thicker year by year, and in the last two years the whole inner side of the leg bulges by evening.

cues: describe the aching in your leg
where exactly do you feel the leg pain
does the pain worsen toward evening
aching_pain.reply: It is a dull aching all over the left leg, worst in the calf and lower leg toward evening. Lying down with the leg on a pillow takes it away by morning.

cues: do your legs feel heavy after duty
tell me about tiredness in the legs
does walking bring any relief
heaviness_tiredness.reply: Both legs feel tired after duty, the left much more. Short slow walks help a little, but standing still at the junction is the worst.

cues: does your ankle swell toward evening
is the swelling gone by next morning
have you noticed pitting near the ankle
ankle_swelling_evening.reply: My left ankle swells by evening and my shoe feels tight. By morning the swelling is nearly gone. Pressing near the ankle leaves a small pit in the evening.

cues: do you get cramps in the leg at night
does cramping disturb your sleep
where do the night cramps strike
night_cramps.reply: Yes, cramps grip my left calf two or three nights a week and wake me. Getting up and walking a little settles them.

cues: is there itching over the lower leg
have you noticed darkening of the ankle skin
any eczema above the ankle bone
skin_itch_pigment.reply: The skin above my inner ankle itches a lot, and it has turned dark brown there. Scratching has made some dry scaly patches.

cues: have you ever had a sore near the ankle
did any ankle wound take long to heal
has the skin ever broken open
venous_ulcer_past.reply: No open sore so far, doctor. Once a scratch near the ankle took nearly a month to dry up, which worried me.

cues: has a vein ever burst and bled
did you ever have sudden bleeding from the leg
how would you manage a burst vein at home
bleed_burst.reply: No bleeding so far. Nobody has told me what to do if a vein bursts, I only know I should come to hospital quickly.

cues: any painful red cord along the veins

skill.gen.appearance.finding: Middle-aged woman, well built, standing with weight shifted to the right leg. No pallor, no distress at rest. Wearing duty boots that leave a deep sock mark above the left ankle.

skill.gen.vitals.finding: Pulse 84 regular. Blood pressure 124/80. Respiratory rate 16. Afebrile. No postural symptoms.

skill.gen.edema.finding: Pitting oedema over the left medial malleolus in the evening clinic, no oedema on the right. Toes slim, dorsum of the foot spared.

skill.exam.surg.varicose_inspection_palp.finding: Standing: tortuous dilated great saphenous trunk from the medial ankle up the inner calf and thigh to the groin on the left. Saphena varix at the groin with an expansile cough impulse. A palpable fascial pit over a medial calf perforator. Brown pigmentation with dry eczema above the medial malleolus, no open ulcer. Right leg shows only a few reticular veins.

skill.exam.surg.trendelenburg_tourniquet.finding: Leg raised and emptied, thumb held at the saphenofemoral junction. On standing the lower veins fill slowly from below despite control; on release a column of blood rushes down from above. Both saphenofemoral and perforator incompetence present.

skill.exam.surg.perthes_deep_vein_patenc.finding: With a thigh tourniquet occluding the surface trunk, brisk walking for five minutes empties the varicosities and the calf stays comfortable with no bursting pain. Deep veins patent.

skill.exam.surg.arterial_pulses_lower.finding: Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses palpable on both feet. No claudication history. Foot warm with normal capillary return.

skill.exam.surg.regional_nodes.finding: No palpable inguinal lymph nodes on either side. No groin hernia. Abdomen soft with no palpable lump.

duplex_venous.label: Duplex ultrasound of both lower limbs
duplex_venous.result: Left great saphenous reflux from the saphenofemoral junction to below the knee with an incompetent Cockett perforator. Deep femoral, popliteal and calf veins patent with competent valves. Right leg shows competent junctions with no truncal reflux.
duplex_venous.note: This is the map the intervention follows: it confirms the hand findings, grades the leak, and proves the deep system is open.

abpi.label: Ankle-brachial pressure index
abpi.result: ABPI 1.02 on the left and 1.04 on the right with audible triphasic signals. No significant arterial disease.
abpi.note: A normal index clears compression and any ulcer care that follows; without it no stocking or bandage should be advised.

bloods_fitness.label: Fitness blood tests
bloods_fitness.result: Haemoglobin 12.4 g per dL. Fasting sugar 96 mg per dL. Urine routine normal. Fit for a day-care procedure.
bloods_fitness.note: Sent because ablation is planned, not to diagnose the veins. An anaemia or sugar finding here would only change fitness, not the diagnosis.

venogram.label: Ascending venography
venogram.note: Not indicated: duplex already maps the reflux and the deep patency. Venography is reserved for deep reconstructions, not for routine varicose planning.

ct_abdomen.label: CT of the abdomen and pelvis
ct_abdomen.note: Not indicated: the abdomen is soft with no lump, onset was gradual over years, and duplex shows primary-pattern disease. Imaging the pelvis is for sudden or one-sided secondary presentations.

d_dimer.label: D-dimer
d_dimer.note: Not indicated: there is no acute whole-leg swelling or calf pain to suggest acute deep vein thrombosis. A number here would only confuse a chronic picture.

differentialModel.answer: Primary varicose veins of the left great saphenous system. Consider deep vein thrombosis with post-thrombotic change, lymphoedema, superficial thrombophlebitis, a venous ulcer diathesis, and peripheral arterial disease sharing the leg.

diagnosis.answer: Primary varicose veins of the left great saphenous system with saphenofemoral and Cockett perforator incompetence, CEAP C4a, deep veins patent, fit for ablation.

managementModel.answer: Graduated compression with leg elevation, exercise and weight advice, duplex-mapped endovenous thermal ablation of the great saphenous trunk with perforator care, emollients for the eczema, bleeding safety-netting, and vascular review with maintenance compression.

teachingPoints: The evening rhythm makes the diagnosis before the leg is exposed: heaviness gathering through standing hours and gone by morning is venous hypertension speaking.
Two phases of one test give two sites: filling from below with the junction held marks the perforators, and the rush from above on release marks the saphenofemoral valve.
A normal Perthes with emptying veins is the permission slip for surface work: it proves the deep system can carry the leg alone.
Pigmentation with eczema above the medial malleolus is CEAP C4a, the last station before ulceration, which is why this case cannot wait on stockings alone.
The abdomen and the deep history are part of every first visit: a soft abdomen with no lump and no past white leg is what lets you call this primary.
Pulses and the arterial index come before compression, not after: a normal ABPI here is what makes the stocking safe.
Her abandoned stockings are a lesson in adherence: compression only works when it is worn, so fit, counsel and follow up rather than merely prescribe.
